paragraphs.english: Every morning, Ben crossed a bridge on his way to school. He usually looked at his phone while walking. One Tuesday, his phone battery was empty, so he watched the river instead. A small white bird stood near the water, and a worker was repairing a sign beside the path. Ben had never noticed either of them before. That afternoon, his art teacher asked students to draw something from their daily journey. Ben drew the bird, the bridge, and the worker's bright hat. His classmates were surprised because they used the same bridge but remembered only the busy road. For the next week, Ben put his phone in his bag during the walk. He saw how the river changed after rain and where flowers grew between stones. He still used his phone at other times. However, he learned that an ordinary journey could offer new things when he paid attention to the world around him.
paragraphs.translation: ベンは毎朝橋を渡って通学し、普段は歩きながらスマホを見ていた。火曜日に電池が切れ、川を見ると白い小鳥や道の標識を直す作業員に初めて気づいた。その午後、美術で毎日の道中の物を描くよう言われ、鳥、橋、作業員の鮮やかな帽子を描いた。同じ橋を使う級友は混雑した道しか覚えておらず驚いた。翌週は歩く間スマホをしまい、雨の後の川の変化や石の間の花を見た。他の時間にはスマホを使うが、周囲に注意すると普通の道でも新しい発見があると学んだ。

paragraphs.english: A bakery near Emma's house became very popular after a local television program introduced it. On Saturdays, customers waited along a narrow street. People who needed to reach other shops found it difficult to pass. The baker wanted to serve everyone, but asking people to stand in a different line did not solve the problem. Emma suggested giving each customer a numbered card. A board by the door showed which numbers could enter. Customers could wait in the nearby square or visit another shop until their turn came. On the back of each card, Emma drew a small map of the square and marked a place to sit. The baker tested the system for two Saturdays. The street became easier to walk through, and several customers said they had discovered shops they had never visited. The bread did not change, but the way people waited improved the whole shopping area. Emma was pleased that her simple idea helped more than one business.

paragraphs.english: For a history project, Tom found a map of his town from fifty years ago. It showed a long road through the center and a lake beside the old station. Tom could still see the road, but he could not find the lake anywhere. He thought the map was wrong. His aunt suggested looking at old photographs in the town office. In one photograph, people were skating on the lake. Another showed workers filling part of it with earth. A town report explained that homes and a new station had later been built there. Tom visited the area again. A short street was still called Lake Road, although no water could be seen. He added photographs and a modern map to his project. Comparing them helped him understand that a familiar town had a history hidden under its present buildings. He also learned to look for more evidence before deciding that an old document was mistaken.

paragraphs.english: When the school bought new chairs, a teacher asked students what to do with the old ones. Some were broken, but many were still strong. Mark suggested sending them all to a recycling center. His friend Nina thought they should first ask whether anyone could use them. The class contacted a children's theater group that practiced in an empty hall. The group needed seats for its audience but could not afford new ones. Students cleaned the strong chairs and checked them with the school caretaker. They sent only the safe ones to the theater. Broken parts went to the recycling center separately. At the first performance, the students sat on chairs they had used for years. The theater leader thanked them for making the hall more welcoming. Mark realized that recycling was useful, but finding a new use for a whole object could sometimes be a better first step. The class began keeping a list of other things people might need.

paragraphs.english: Lucy loved buying beautiful notebooks. She had five at home, but most pages were empty. She wanted each notebook to contain perfect writing and neat pictures. Whenever she made a spelling mistake on the first page, she stopped using that notebook. One day, her older brother showed her a notebook from his first year at college. It contained crossed-out words, arrows, rough drawings, and questions without answers. He explained that it helped him work through difficult ideas. A notebook did not have to be a finished book for other people to admire. Lucy chose one of her empty notebooks and wrote a plan for a school play. When a scene did not work, she crossed it out and tried another. A month later, the pages looked messy, but her play was ready. She felt more proud of that used notebook than of the clean ones on her shelf. Mistakes had become signs of progress rather than reasons to stop.

paragraphs.english: A walking club planned a trip along a forest path. The leader, Sam, knew the route well and thought everyone could finish it in two hours. On the first practice walk, however, the group soon spread out. Some members stopped to take pictures, while others walked slowly on the steep parts. The fastest members reached the end without seeing the rest of the group for almost an hour. Sam realized that knowing a path was not the same as planning a good group trip. Before the next walk, he asked members about their pace and interests. He marked three meeting points and chose someone to walk at the back. The group also agreed on a signal for asking for a rest. The second walk took longer, but everyone reached the end together and shared what they had noticed. Sam learned that a successful trip should be measured by the group's experience, not just by the time on his own watch.

paragraphs.english: A community center invited local families to a free music evening. The staff posted a colorful invitation on social media and expected a large audience. Only twelve people came. At first, the manager thought families were not interested in music. A volunteer named Amy asked visitors at the center how they usually learned about events. Some checked social media every day, but others read the board at the bus stop or looked for notices in their children's school bags. A few people did not know that the center's social media page existed. For the next music evening, the staff used several ways to share the same information. paragraphs.english: Mia saved money to buy a small desk lamp. At a shop, she found two lamps that looked almost the same. One was cheaper, so she was ready to buy it. Her father asked her to read the information on both boxes first. The cheaper lamp needed a special kind of battery that the shop did not sell. The other could use ordinary batteries or connect to a wall socket. Mia also checked whether a broken part could be replaced and how long the shop would accept returns. She did not simply choose the more expensive lamp because her father mentioned it. Instead, she wrote down the costs and features that mattered to her. In the end, she chose the second lamp because she planned to use it at her desk every evening. The experience taught her that a price label was only one part of a buying decision. Asking the right questions helped her spend her savings more carefully.

paragraphs.english: The photography club held a meeting where each member showed one picture. Most students brought their best work. Alex brought a photograph that was too dark. Some members wondered why he had chosen it. Alex explained that he liked the shape of the trees but had used the wrong camera setting. He wanted advice about taking the same scene again. The discussion became more lively than usual. One student suggested a different time of day, and another showed how to change a setting. Soon other members began sharing pictures that had not turned out well. The club adviser said that showing success could encourage people, but showing an unfinished attempt could invite useful help. The following month, the club added a short session called Work in Progress. Members still celebrated their best pictures, but they no longer felt that every meeting had to be a competition. Alex returned to the trees and took a clearer photograph with ideas he had learned from his friends.

paragraphs.english: Two schools in different towns started an online book club. The teachers chose the same short novel for both groups. At the first meeting, students tried to discuss the whole book at once. The conversation moved quickly, and several students who had read carefully said very little. For the second meeting, the teachers asked each group to bring one question and one favorite passage. They sent these to the other school two days before the call. Students had time to think and look at the book again. During the meeting, they discovered that they understood one character's choice differently. Instead of arguing about who was right, they pointed to words in the story and explained their reasons. The meeting ended with more questions than it had started with, but everyone wanted to read the next book. The teachers were happy because the club had become a place for careful conversation rather than a test of who could answer fastest.
paragraphs.translation: 別の町の二校でオンライン読書会を始め、同じ短い小説を読んだ。初回は全体を一度に話そうとして会話が速く、よく読んだのに黙る生徒もいた。次回は質問一つと好きな一節を二日前に交換し、考え読み直す時間を作った。ある人物の選択の理解が違うと気づくと、どちらが正しいか争わず本文の語句を示して理由を説明した。問いは増えたが皆次の本を読みたがった。先生たちは最速回答の試験でなく、丁寧な対話の場になったことを喜んだ。
